frame.objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.
Alternatives include expanding the existing professional line, creating a new consumer product, targeting a different customer segment, or maintaining the current portfolio.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home barista, travel, or small office) with a new product or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing professional line with consumer‑focused features (e.g., simplified controls, compact design) without creating a new product.
3) Target a different customer segment (e.g., coffee shops, hotels, or retail consumers) with a differentiated offering, leveraging existing or new distribution channels.
4) Maintain the current portfolio and not pursue expansion, focusing resources on existing professional and commercial segments.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a premium, design-driven experience that reflects personal style and quality, leading them to purchase multiple units or premium accessories.
T1.who_benefits: Simonelli Group benefits by capturing higher margins through premium pricing and repeat purchases of accessories.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from viewing coffee as a utility to a lifestyle product when they associate a machine with personal expression and quality, prompting them to own multiple units or upgrade.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Simonelli can capture value through premium pricing, direct-to-consumer sales, and recurring revenue from accessories and maintenance.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for design and quality.
Simonelli can effectively communicate the premium positioning to consumers.
The market size for premium home espresso machines is sufficient to justify investment.
predictions: Consumers will express higher willingness to pay for a differentiated consumer proposition compared to a standard professional line.
Sales of premium accessories and multiple units will increase in the target segment.
Survey data will show that design and personal expression are primary purchase drivers for consumers.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a premium, design-driven experience that reflects personal style and quality, leading them to purchase multiple units or premium accessories.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a convenient, time-saving solution for busy lifestyles, leading them to purchase a compact or automated machine that simplifies coffee preparation.
T2.who_benefits: Simonelli Group benefits by capturing value through higher volume sales of compact models and recurring revenue from maintenance and accessories.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers with limited time shift from viewing coffee as a chore to a convenience task, prompting them to choose machines that automate or simplify preparation.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Simonelli can capture value through increased unit sales of compact models, premium pricing for convenience features, and recurring revenue from accessories and service contracts.
assumptions: Time constraints are a primary purchase driver for consumers.
Compact or automated machines offer a clear convenience advantage over traditional professional machines.
Simonelli can design and market a compact machine that meets consumer convenience expectations.
predictions: Consumers will show higher purchase intent for compact machines compared to standard professional machines.
Sales of compact models will increase in the target segment.
Survey data will show that convenience and time savings are primary purchase drivers for consumers.

position.recommendation: Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition built on the existing combi‑steamer technology, emphasizing convenience, time‑saving, and cleanup reduction. The evidence shows RATIONAL already serves professional and commercial customers, but its market potential includes 4.8 million customers, 75% of whom still use traditional cooking appliances. This suggests a large, untapped home‑cook market that could benefit.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

T1.claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer because it simplifies meal preparation, reduces cleanup, and saves time, leading them to purchase a premium, smart device.
T1.who_benefits: Home cooks seeking convenience and efficiency in cooking.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Time constraints and desire for faster, cleaner cooking make the combi-steamer an attractive alternative to traditional methods.
T1.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL can charge a premium price for a smart, compact model and capture recurring revenue through accessories and software updates.
assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay more for a device that reduces cooking time and cleanup.
Smart features and connectivity are valued by the target segment.
Distribution channels can reach home cooks effectively.
predictions: Surveyed home cooks will express intent to purchase a combi-steamer at a higher rate than professional kitchen users.
Willingness to pay will be higher for a smart, compact model compared to a standard combi-steamer.

Marketing can effectively communicate the professional image.
predictions: Home cooks will show higher purchase intent for a premium, professional-looking combi-steamer compared to a standard model.

X1.name: Convenience vs. Status Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from home cooks (self-identified) and professional kitchen users. Each participant views a product description of a RATIONAL combi-steamer and is asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR). Messaging is randomized between a convenience framing (time-saving, cleanup reduction) and a status framing (professional‑grade, premium).
X1.sample: 500 participants: 250 home cooks (self‑identified) and 250 professional kitchen users. Recruit via panel to ensure demographic balance.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and average willingness to pay (EUR) for each frame.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Home cooks will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the convenience frame than for the status frame.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Home cooks will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay for the status frame than for the convenience frame.

X1.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay for the convenience frame exceeds the status frame by ≥ €50, recommend developing a differentiated home‑cook proposition focused on convenience. If the status frame exceeds the convenience frame by ≥ €50, recommend a premium, status‑focused offering. If neither difference meets the thresholds, recommend no expansion (maintain current B2B focus).

final.recommendation: Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition built on the existing combi‑steamer technology, emphasizing convenience, time‑saving, and cleanup reduction. The evidence shows RATIONAL already serves professional and commercial customers, but its market potential includes 4.8 million customers, 75% of whom still use traditional cooking appliances. This suggests a large, untapped home‑cook market that could benefit.
final.target_customer: Home cooks who value convenience, efficiency, and faster meal preparation.
final.value_proposition: A compact, smart combi‑steamer that simplifies cooking, reduces cleanup, and saves time, offering a premium price point and recurring revenue through accessories and software updates.
final.next_action: Run the proposed convenience‑vs‑status messaging test (or a smaller pilot) to validate willingness to pay and purchase intent for the convenience framing. If the test meets the thresholds, proceed to develop the home‑cook offering; if not,
final.uncertainty: The exact size of the home‑cook market and the specific drivers of purchase intent (convenience vs. status) remain uncertain. The test results will clarify whether home cooks are willing to pay a premium for convenience features.
would_change_if: If the test shows the status framing generates significantly higher willingness to pay than the convenience framing, we would reconsider a premium, status‑focused offering.
If the test fails to show a meaningful difference between the two frames, we would recommend no expansion and maintain the current B2B focus.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

T1.claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is marketed as a smart, subscription-based device that automates cooking and delivers recipes, because they value convenience and recurring revenue.
T1.who_benefits: Home cooks seeking time-saving, automated cooking solutions.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They would switch from traditional cooking methods to a device that simplifies meal preparation and offers ongoing content and service fees.
T1.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL would capture value through recurring subscription fees, premium pricing for smart features, and data-driven personalized recommendations.
assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay recurring fees for convenience.
Smart home integration and connectivity are acceptable to residential users.
RATIONAL can develop and market a subscription-ready product within budget.
predictions: A pilot offering a subscription-based combi-steamer will generate at least 10% monthly recurring revenue within 12 weeks.
Surveyed home cooks will indicate willingness to pay €150/month for the device plus subscription fees.
Adoption rate among surveyed home cooks will be at least 15%.
T1.first_claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is marketed as a smart, subscription-based device that automates cooking and delivers recipes, because they value convenience and recurring revenue.

T2.claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is positioned as a premium, high-performance professional-grade device that offers superior cooking precision and durability, because they value professional-quality results and are willing to pay a premium.
T2.who_benefits: Home cooks who prioritize professional cooking outcomes and are willing to invest in high-end appliances.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: They would switch from lower-cost consumer appliances to a device that delivers consistent, professional results, justifying the higher price.
T2.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL would capture value through premium pricing, limited-edition designs, and brand positioning as a professional-grade brand.
assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay a premium for professional-grade performance.
Professional-grade branding and design are perceived as a differentiator.
RATIONAL can maintain or enhance its premium brand image while scaling production.
predictions: A premium-priced combi-steamer will achieve at least 15% higher average transaction value than a comparable low-priced model.
Surveyed home cooks will rank professional-grade performance as the top purchase criterion for 60% of respondents.
Sales of the premium model will increase by at least 20% in the first 12 months after launch.

position.recommendation: Develop a differentiated subscription-based combi-steamer proposition for home cooks, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing B2B relationships and subscription model to capture recurring revenue.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

T1.claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is marketed as a smart, subscription-based device that simplifies meal preparation, because they value convenience and recurring revenue.
T1.who_benefits: Home cooks seeking time-saving cooking solutions and subscription services.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: A subscription model reduces upfront cost and provides ongoing updates, making the product more attractive than a one-time purchase.
T1.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL can capture value through recurring subscription fees and premium pricing for smart features, while also leveraging its existing B2B relationships to reach consumers.
assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay a subscription fee for convenience.
The smart features are perceived as valuable enough to justify the subscription cost.
RATIONAL can integrate a subscription platform into its existing product line without significant additional development.
predictions: In a test offering a subscription-based combi-steamer, at least 30% of respondents will sign up within 6 weeks.
Surveyed home cooks will report a willingness to pay a monthly fee of €20-€30 for the device.
Adoption rates will be higher among younger, tech-savvy consumers compared to older demographics.
T1.first_claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is marketed as a smart, subscription-based device that simplifies meal preparation, because they value convenience and recurring revenue.

T2.claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is positioned as a premium, high-performance appliance that signals professional quality and status, because they view cooking as a lifestyle and are willing to pay for brand prestige.
T2.who_benefits: Home cooks who value brand prestige, professional-grade performance, and status signaling.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: A premium positioning creates a perception of higher quality and exclusivity, leading consumers to choose the product over cheaper alternatives.
T2.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL can capture value through premium pricing, limited-edition designs, and brand marketing that emphasizes professional heritage, while also leveraging its existing B2B reputation to attract home consumers.
assumptions: Home cooks are price-sensitive and prioritize brand perception over cost.
Professional-grade performance is a key purchase driver for home cooks.
RATIONAL can effectively communicate its professional heritage to home consumers without diluting its commercial image.
predictions: In a test offering a premium-priced combi-steamer, at least 25% of respondents will choose it over a lower-priced alternative.
Surveyed home cooks will report willingness to pay at least 20% more for a product marketed as "professional-grade" compared to a standard model.
Adoption rates will be higher among consumers who already own professional-grade kitchen equipment.
T2.first_claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is positioned as a premium, high-performance appliance that signals professional quality and status, because they view cooking as a lifestyle and are willing to pay for brand prestige.

X1.name: Subscription vs Premium Positioning Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 500 German adults (250 per arm) recruited via panel, balanced for age, gender, and cooking frequency.
X1.measure: 1) WTP: maximum monthly fee (EUR) a respondent would pay for the device. 2) Choice: percentage selecting "Subscription" vs "Premium" option. 3) Intent to purchase: binary (would buy).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Subscription arm shows higher WTP and higher "Subscription" choice than Premium arm; Premium arm shows low intent.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Premium arm shows higher WTP and higher "Premium" choice than Subscription arm; Subscription arm shows low intent.

X1.decision_rule: If Subscription arm WTP ≥ €30 and Premium arm WTP < €20, recommend Subscription positioning (T1). Else if Premium arm WTP ≥ €30 and Subscription arm WTP < €20, recommend Premium positioning (T2). If neither condition is met, inconclusive and no expansion.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence about a label printer reducing packing errors does not address home cook demand, subscription willingness, or premium positioning, so it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Develop a differentiated subscription-based combi-steamer proposition for home cooks, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing B2B relationships and subscription model to capture recurring revenue.
final.target_customer: Home cooks who value convenience, time-saving solutions, and recurring revenue, particularly younger, tech-savvy consumers.
final.value_proposition: A subscription-based combi-steamer that reduces upfront cost and provides ongoing updates, while RATIONAL captures value through recurring subscription fees and premium pricing for smart features.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Subscription vs Premium Positioning Test (500 German adults, 8 weeks, €15,000) to measure willingness-to-pay and purchase intent for subscription versus premium positioning.
final.uncertainty: The size of the home cook market and their willingness to pay for a subscription model are unknown. The test will resolve whether subscription demand is sufficient to justify expansion.
would_change_if: If the test shows subscription WTP < €20 and premium WTP ≥ €30, we would shift to premium positioning (T2).
If the test shows no significant difference between subscription and premium arms, we would recommend no expansion and stay focused on professional kitchens.
If new evidence shows strong home cook demand for professional-grade status, we would reconsider premium positioning.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

T1.claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is marketed as a smart, subscription-based device that automates cooking and delivers recipes, because they value convenience and recurring revenue.
T1.who_benefits: Home cooks seeking time-saving, automated cooking solutions.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Smart features and subscription model reduce manual effort and provide ongoing content, making the appliance attractive for daily use.
T1.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL can charge a monthly subscription for recipe access, software updates, and premium features, generating recurring revenue while leveraging its existing combi-steamer technology.
assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay a recurring fee for smart cooking features.
The subscription model is feasible without significant additional hardware costs.
Competitors do not offer a comparable subscription-based model.
predictions: A pilot offering a subscription-based combi-steamer will achieve at least 10% monthly subscription conversion among targeted home cooks.
Surveyed adopters will report higher satisfaction with automated cooking compared to traditional appliances.
T1.first_claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is marketed as a smart, subscription-based device that automates cooking and delivers recipes, because they value convenience and recurring revenue.

T2.claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is marketed as a premium, high-performance appliance that emphasizes precision cooking and professional-grade results, because they value quality and performance.
T2.who_benefits: Home cooks who cook frequently and seek professional-quality results.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Premium positioning and performance claims create a perception of superior cooking capability, motivating purchase despite higher price.
T2.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL can command premium pricing and differentiate itself in a market where performance is a key purchase driver, leveraging its existing technology to justify higher margins.
assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay a premium for perceived superior performance.
The premium positioning can be effectively communicated without overwhelming the product.
Competitors do not offer comparable premium positioning.
predictions: A premium-priced combi-steamer will achieve at least 15% higher average transaction value compared to a comparable low-priced model.
Surveyed adopters will cite performance and precision as the primary reason for purchasing.
T2.first_claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is marketed as a premium, high-performance appliance that emphasizes precision cooking and professional-grade results, because they value quality and performance.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes cost savings and uptime for multi‑family buildings and shared spaces, supported by evidence that residential customers increasingly demand commercial‑quality home products.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and the feasibility of reaching it.
Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).
2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.
4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).
5) Target a different customer group within the professional segment (e.g., small hotels, gyms, or healthcare facilities) with a differentiated proposition.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt self‑service laundry solutions if they perceive lower operational costs and higher uptime, leading them to purchase dedicated machines for multi‑family buildings, student housing, and other shared spaces.
T1.who_benefits: Residents, guests, and members in multi‑family buildings and shared facilities benefit from reduced labor costs and increased machine uptime.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from hiring laundry services to self‑service machines when they calculate that the upfront cost is offset by long‑term savings and reduced downtime.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Electrolux captures value by selling premium‑priced machines and offering service contracts that ensure uptime and performance.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for machines that reduce long‑term operational costs.
Uptime and reliability are critical decision factors for consumers.
Electrolux can deliver on the performance claims and provide service support.
predictions: In a survey, consumers will indicate that they would choose a self‑service machine if it promises at least a 10% reduction in monthly laundry costs compared to a traditional laundromat.
Willingness to pay for a self‑service machine will be higher when paired with a warranty covering downtime.
Adoption rates will be higher in multi‑family buildings and student housing than in single‑family homes.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt self‑service laundry solutions if they perceive lower operational costs and higher uptime, leading them to purchase dedicated machines for multi‑family buildings, student housing, and other shared spaces.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt self‑service laundry solutions if they perceive the convenience of running their own laundry, reducing the need to wait for a laundromat or hire a service, leading them to purchase machines for multi‑family buildings and shared spaces.
T2.who_benefits: Residents, guests, and members in multi‑family buildings and shared facilities benefit from the convenience of self‑service laundry.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from relying on external laundry services to self‑service machines when convenience becomes a primary decision factor, especially in spaces where time and effort are limited.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Electrolux captures value by selling machines that are easy to operate and integrate with existing building infrastructure, and by offering support services that ensure smooth operation.
assumptions: Consumers value time savings and convenience over cost savings.
Self‑service machines are perceived as user‑friendly and easy to operate.
Electrolux can provide clear instructions and support for consumers.
predictions: In a survey, consumers will rank convenience as the top reason for choosing a self‑service machine, above cost or uptime.
Adoption rates will be higher in multi‑family buildings and student housing than in single‑family homes.
Consumers will be willing to pay a premium for machines that offer a simple, one‑button operation.

There were 32 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 72 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and the feasibility of reaching it.
Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).
2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.
4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).
5) Target a different customer group within the professional segment (e.g., small hotels, gyms, or healthcare facilities) with a differentiated proposition.

X1.name: Consumer preference test for differentiated home laundry proposition
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two versions of a consumer‑operated laundry unit (one emphasizing convenience and cost savings, the other emphasizing energy efficiency and long‑term cost savings). Participants are recruited from homeowners who have used professional laundry services and are interested in home laundry solutions. Each participant sees one version for 2 minutes and then indicates willingness to pay a premium (20% over the base unit price) and intent to purchase.
X1.sample: 400 homeowners (200 per arm) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, income, and prior experience with professional laundry services.
X1.measure: Primary measure: share of participants willing to pay the premium price (20% above base unit price). Secondary measure: stated reason for choosing the version (convenience vs. energy efficiency).

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 30% of participants will choose the convenience version and express willingness to pay the premium price.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 25% of participants will choose the energy‑efficiency version and express willingness to pay the premium price.

X1.decision_rule: If the convenience version achieves at least 30% willingness to pay and the energy‑efficiency version achieves at most 25%, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing convenience. If the energy‑efficiency version achieves at least 25% willingness to pay and the convenience version at most 30%, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing energy efficiency. If neither version reaches the respective threshold, do not expand into a differentiated consumer proposition.

revisions.reason: The simulated result (SYN-EPRO-UPDATE) tests the incremental effect of durability and repairability versus performance and price in a recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. It does not address T1's core claim about homeowners' willingness to pay a premium for convenience and cost savings. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not yet commit to a differentiated consumer proposition. Public evidence shows residential customers are demanding commercial-quality home products and that professional customers can reach consumers through retail and wholesale channels. A test is needed to measure willingness to pay for convenience versus energy efficiency.
final.target_customer: Homeowners and small businesses seeking convenient, affordable laundry solutions.
final.value_proposition: A consumer‑operated laundry unit that offers convenience and cost savings (or energy‑efficiency and long‑term cost savings) through a differentiated brand and direct sales channel.
final.next_action: Run the proposed consumer preference test (400 homeowners, 8 weeks, €18,000) to compare willingness to pay for convenience versus energy‑efficiency versions.
final.uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay for convenience versus energy efficiency is unknown; the test will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the test shows the energy‑efficiency version achieving at least 25% willingness to pay, the recommendation would shift to emphasize energy efficiency.
If neither version reaches the respective threshold, the recommendation would remain to not expand into a differentiated consumer proposition.

tool_result.title: Simulated durability-and-repairability proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 32 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 72 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and the feasibility of reaching it.
Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).
2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.
4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).
5) Target a different customer group within the professional segment (e.g., small hotels, gyms, or healthcare facilities) with a differentiated proposition.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they view the product as a convenience and resource efficiency solution for their home or small business, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners, small business owners, and renters seeking reliable, space-saving laundry solutions.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing demand for commercial-quality home appliances and convenience in multi‑family buildings and student housing creates a need for a product that simplifies laundry tasks and reduces downtime.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Electrolux can capture value through premium pricing for a differentiated model, bundled service contracts, and direct‑to‑consumer sales channels that leverage its existing professional brand credibility.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that improves convenience and resource efficiency.
Electrolux can reach consumers through existing retail and wholesale channels without significant new investment.
The product meets consumer expectations for reliability and performance comparable to professional models.
predictions: In a test offering a differentiated consumer model to homeowners in a target market, purchase intent will be at least 20% higher than a baseline offering of a standard professional model.
Surveyed consumers will rank convenience and resource efficiency as top reasons for choosing the product, with willingness to pay at least 15% above the price of a comparable professional model.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they view the product as a convenience and resource efficiency solution for their home or small business, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if it is positioned as a premium, brand‑driven product that offers superior performance and design, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners and small business owners who value brand prestige, design aesthetics, and perceived quality.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Growing consumer awareness of brand reputation and desire for stylish, high‑performance home appliances creates a need for a product that stands out in a crowded market.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Electrolux can capture value through premium pricing, limited‑edition designs, and direct‑to‑consumer branding that leverages its professional brand credibility.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that is perceived as a premium brand.
Electrolux can effectively communicate brand value through marketing and retail positioning.
The product meets or exceeds consumer expectations for performance and design.
predictions: In a test offering a premium‑positioned consumer model to homeowners, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher than a baseline offering of a standard professional model.
Surveyed consumers will rank brand prestige and design as top reasons for choosing the product, with willingness to pay at least 20% above the price of a comparable professional model.
T2.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if it is positioned as a premium, brand‑driven product that offers superior performance and design, leading to higher purchase intent and willingness to pay.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and the feasibility of reaching it.
Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).
2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.
4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).

X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to a consumer‑oriented self‑service laundry unit (premium price) and a business‑oriented unit (premium price). Participants are recruited from homeowners (n=300) and small businesses (n=300). Each participant views a product description and is asked to indicate likelihood to purchase at the premium price.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent than small businesses.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent among homeowners exceeds small businesses by at least 10 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. final.uncertainty: The willingness of homeowners to pay a premium for consumer‑operated solutions is unknown. Small‑business demand and willingness to pay are also uncertain.
would_change_if: If the test shows small‑business purchase intent exceeds homeowners by at least 10 percentage points, we would shift focus to a small‑business proposition.

result.title: Simulated durability-and-repairability proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 household washing-machine buyers eligible for the same professional-derived washer offer were assigned equally to two descriptions. Both descriptions showed the same machine, brand, price, warranty, availability, service terms and verified specifications. One emphasized durability and repairability; the other emphasized washing performance and the upfront price. No discount or extra service was added. The outcome was a paid, refundable purchase reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned buyers per arm. There were 72 reservations in the durability-and-repairability description arm and 32 in the performance-and-price description arm. This tests the incremental effect of the description in this recruited population, not actual appliance lifetime, delivery capability, market size, profitability or sustained repurchase. A weaker result would not refute a different channel or product theory.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners, leveraging Electron‑x’s professional‑grade reputation and existing consumer‑operated solutions. Begin with a limited pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Electron’x Professional Group investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional laundry offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and competitive positioning.
Must consider existing consumer reach (if any) and the feasibility of reaching it.
Any recommendation must be based on observable demand, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home laundry, small businesses, or a new segment).
2) Expand the existing professional offering into adjacent consumer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., add consumer‑focused features to professional models).
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on professional laundry and food‑service equipment.
4) Change the route to market for existing professional products to reach consumers directly (e.g., online sales, retail partnerships).
5) Target a different customer group within the professional segment (e.g., small hotels, gyms, or healthcare facilities) with a differentiated proposition.

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt consumer‑operated laundry solutions because they seek convenience, cost savings, and the ability to manage their own laundry, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners gain direct control over laundry timing and cost; Electron‑x gains a new revenue stream and brand extension.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Growing home‑laundry complexity and desire for flexibility make self‑service appealing; homeowners are willing to pay a premium for convenience and reduced dependency on third‑party services.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Electrolux can capture value through direct consumer sales, premium pricing, and recurring services, leveraging its professional‑grade reputation to build trust.
assumptions: Homeowners have sufficient disposable income to purchase a self‑service unit.
Regulatory and safety standards can be adapted for consumer use.
Distribution channels (e.g., retail, online) are accessible to reach homeowners.
predictions: In a test offering a consumer‑operated unit to homeowners, purchase intent or actual purchase rate will exceed a baseline of 10% among surveyed homeowners.
Willingness to pay will be at least 20% above the price of a comparable professional unit, indicating premium acceptance.

T2.why_behaviour_changes: Small businesses face high laundry costs and downtime, making self‑service a financially attractive option; they prioritize reliability and efficiency over convenience alone.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Electrolux can capture value through volume sales, recurring service contracts, and premium pricing justified by reliability, leveraging its professional‑grade reputation to build trust.

X1.name: Consumer vs Business Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized exposure to a consumer‑operated unit (home use) and a business‑oriented unit (small business use). Participants are randomly assigned to view either the consumer or business description. They are then asked: “Would you purchase this unit?” (binary) and “What is your maximum price you would pay?” (willingness to pay).
X1.sample: 300 respondents: 150 homeowners (recruited via home‑laundry forums) and 150 small‑business owners (recruited via trade associations). Stratify by region to ensure geographic diversity.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and willingness to pay (percentage of respondents offering a price).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than small‑business owners, indicating demand for convenience.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Small‑business owners will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than homeowners, indicating demand for cost‑efficiency.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent for the consumer unit exceeds that for the business unit by at least 10 percentage points among homeowners, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If purchase intent for the business unit exceeds that for the consumer unit by at least 10 percentage points among small‑business owners, develop a differentiated B2B proposition. If neither difference is significant, do not expand into consumer markets.

revisions.reason: The simulated result (SYN-EPRO-UPDATE) tests the incremental effect of durability-and-repairability versus performance-and-price descriptions among household buyers, not actual purchase behavior. It does not address T1, which predicts homeowners will adopt self-service solutions due to convenience and cost savings. Therefore T1 remains unchanged.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners, leveraging Electron‑x’s professional‑grade reputation and existing consumer‑operated solutions. Begin with a limited pilot to test purchase intent and willingness to pay before scaling.
final.target_customer: Homeowners in multi‑family buildings, student housing, and similar residential settings who seek convenience, cost savings, and direct control over laundry timing.
final.value_proposition: A consumer‑operated laundry unit that combines professional‑grade reliability, easy self‑service operation, and optional premium features (e.g., smart connectivity, extended warranty) to deliver convenience and peace of mind.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Business Purchase Intent Test (300 respondents, 8 weeks, €18,000) to validate demand. If purchase intent for the consumer unit exceeds that for the business unit by at least 10 percentage points among homeowners
final.uncertainty: The actual willingness to pay premium and the size of the homeowner market remain uncertain. Evidence of strong consumer demand is limited to the company‑assertion that consumer‑operated setups exist, and no source shows homeowners will pay
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the consumer unit is no higher than 10 percentage points than for the business unit, indicating weak demand, the recommendation would shift toward no expansion or a different route to market.
If new evidence shows homeowners are unwilling to pay a premium for self‑service units, the case for a differentiated consumer proposition would weaken.

X1.name: Consumer vs Business Purchase Intent Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are randomly assigned to either a homeowner group (n=200) or a small business/housing provider group (n=200). Each group sees a product description of a consumer‑operated machine (e.g., compact washing/drying unit) and a professional‑grade machine. Homeowners are asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay. Small‑business/housing providers are asked to indicate purchase intent and whether they would purchase at a given price point. The test also includes a follow‑up survey to measure repeat service usage.
X1.sample: 200 homeowners and 200 small businesses/housing providers, recruited via an online panel to match demographic distribution.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) for each group and average price willingness to pay. Secondary measure: repeat service usage (binary: ≥ 3 cycles per year).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Homeowners will show higher purchase intent and be willing to pay a premium for the consumer‑operated machine than small‑business/housing providers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Small‑business/housing providers will show higher purchase intent and be willing to pay a premium for the consumer‑operated machine than homeowners.

X1.decision_rule: If homeowners’ purchase intent ≥ 7 and their average price willingness to pay ≥ €400, and small‑business/housing providers’ purchase intent ≤ 5, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners. If small‑business/housing providers’ purchase intent ≥ 7 and their average price willingness to pay ≥ €400, proceed to develop a differentiated proposition targeting small businesses. If neither threshold is met, do not expand.

revisions.reason: The simulated result (SYN-EPRO-UPDATE) tests the incremental effect of durability and repairability versus performance and price descriptions among a recruited household washing-machine buyer population. It does not address homeowners’ willingness to pay a premium for consumer‑operated machines, so it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Public evidence shows residential customers are demanding commercial-quality home laundry, but it does not demonstrate homeowners will purchase or pay a premium for consumer‑operated machines. A limited test (e.g., purchase intent survey) is needed to validate demand before committing resources.

final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer vs Business Purchase Intent Test (or a similar survey) to measure purchase intent and price willingness among homeowners and small‑business/housing providers. Use the decision rule to decide whether to proceed with
final.uncertainty: The willingness of homeowners to pay a premium for consumer‑operated machines is uncertain. Public evidence does not show purchase intent or price elasticity, and the test budget is limited to €20,000 and 12‑week timeline.
would_change_if: If the test shows homeowners’ purchase intent ≥ 7 and average price willingness to pay ≥ €400, we would proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting homeowners.
If small‑business/housing providers show higher purchase intent and price willingness to pay, we would consider a proposition targeting small businesses.
If neither group meets the thresholds, we would recommend no expansion.

arguments.sample: 200 homeowners and 200 small businesses/housing providers, recruited via an online panel to match demographic distribution.

X1.name: Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test
X1.method: Online controlled experiment with two product variants of the same Aquaporin membrane purifier. Participants are randomly assigned to view either a premium positioning message (highlighting superior taste and purity) or a sustainability positioning message (highlighting reduced plastic waste). After viewing the message, participants indicate purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to ensure representative exposure.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and maximum price willingness to pay (continuous). Secondary measure: self-reported importance of taste/purity vs sustainability.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants exposed to premium positioning will have higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than those exposed to sustainability positioning.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants exposed to sustainability positioning will have higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than those exposed to premium positioning.

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two conditions is at least 10 percentage points and the sustainability condition exceeds the premium condition by at least 5 percentage points, proceed with the sustainability-focused differentiated proposition. If the premium condition exceeds the sustainability condition by at least 5 percentage points, proceed with the premium positioning. If neither condition meets the thresholds, do not launch a differentiated proposition and continue focusing on existing B2B membranes.

arguments.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if they perceive it as a premium, health‑focused product that offers superior taste and purity, leading them to pay a premium price.
arguments.who_benefits: Health‑conscious consumers seeking higher purity and better taste in drinking water.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers shift from viewing water purifiers as a necessity to a lifestyle or health product, they will be willing to purchase a premium‑priced purifier that justifies the cost.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Aquaporin can capture value by pricing the differentiated product at a premium, selling through direct‑to‑consumer channels or premium retailers, and leveraging brand positioning as a premium water‑purification solution.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for perceived health and taste benefits.
The premium positioning can be effectively communicated to the target segment.
Distribution channels can reach the premium segment without significant cost.
predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.
Surveyed consumers will rank taste and purity as top reasons for purchasing the premium product.

arguments.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if it is marketed as a sustainable, eco‑friendly product that reduces plastic waste, leading them to choose it over conventional purifiers.
arguments.who_benefits: Environmentally conscious consumers who prioritize reducing single‑use plastic consumption.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers associate water purifiers with sustainability and waste reduction, they will be motivated to switch from existing products, even if the cost is higher.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Aquaporin can capture value by positioning the product as a sustainable solution, pricing it at a premium for eco‑conscious buyers, and selling through channels that emphasize environmental messaging.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for a product that reduces plastic waste.
Environmental messaging can effectively influence purchase decisions.
Distribution channels can highlight sustainability attributes without compromising margins.
predictions: In a test offering a sustainability‑focused differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.
Surveyed consumers will rank sustainability as a top reason for purchasing the product.

arguments.name: Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online controlled experiment with two product variants of the same Aquaporin membrane purifier. Participants are randomly assigned to view either a premium positioning message (highlighting superior taste and purity) or a sustainability positioning message (highlighting reduced plastic waste). After viewing the message, participants indicate purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price they would pay.
arguments.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to ensure representative exposure.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and maximum price willingness to pay (continuous). Secondary measure: self-reported importance of taste/purity vs sustainability.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants exposed to premium positioning will have higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than those exposed to sustainability positioning.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants exposed to sustainability positioning will have higher purchase intent and higher willingness to pay than those exposed to premium positioning.

arguments.decision_rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two conditions is at least 10 percentage points and the sustainability condition exceeds the premium condition by at least 5 percentage points, proceed with the sustainability-focused differentiated proposition. If the premium condition exceeds the sustainability condition by at least 5 percentage points, proceed with the premium positioning. If neither condition meets the thresholds, do not launch a differentiated proposition and continue focusing on existing B2B membranes.

result.title: Simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the product as a premium, health-focused water purifier, leveraging Aquaporin's existing user-friendly design and brand reputation. Begin with a limited launch in a specific segment (e.g., health-conscious households) to test demand before broader rollout.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Aquaporin A/S investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current water-membrane offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a viable route to market for a differentiated consumer proposition.
Any recommendation must be based on observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home water purifier for a niche segment).
2) Expand the existing water‑membrane offering to new markets or customer segments without a differentiated proposition (e.g., B2B expansion).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on current B2B membranes and existing distribution channels.
4) Change the route to market (e.g., direct‑to‑consumer e‑commerce, partnerships with retailers) without altering the product proposition.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated home water purifier if they perceive it as a premium, health‑focused product that offers superior taste and purity, leading them to pay a premium price.
T1.who_benefits: Health‑conscious consumers seeking higher purity and better taste in drinking water.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers shift from viewing water purifiers as a necessity to a lifestyle or health product, they will be willing to purchase a premium‑priced purifier that justifies the cost.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Aquaporin can capture value by pricing the differentiated product at a premium, selling through direct‑to‑consumer channels or premium retailers, and leveraging brand positioning as a premium water‑purification solution.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for perceived health and taste benefits.
The premium positioning can be effectively communicated to the target segment.
Distribution channels can reach the premium segment without significant cost.
predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.
Surveyed consumers will rank taste and purity as top reasons for purchasing the premium product.

X1.name: Premium vs. Sustainability Messaging Test
X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with simulated purchase decision. Participants view two product concepts (standard water purifier and a differentiated version) and indicate which they would purchase and the maximum price they would pay. Messaging is randomized: premium health messaging (taste, purity) vs. sustainability messaging (plastic waste reduction).
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region to reflect a broad European market.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and maximum willingness-to-pay (WTP) for each concept.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher average WTP for the premium health messaging version compared to the sustainability messaging version.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher average WTP for the sustainability messaging version compared to the premium health messaging version.

X1.decision_rule: If the premium health messaging version achieves at least 15% higher purchase intent and at least 10% higher average WTP than the sustainability messaging version, proceed with a differentiated premium health proposition. revisions.reason: The simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test (SYN-AQP-UPDATE) does not address consumer perception of taste, purity, or willingness to pay a premium for a differentiated product. It tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under a conditional supply assumption, which is unrelated to membrane efficacy, long-term filter use, or market size. Therefore, the evidence does not support or contradict T1.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that positions the product as a premium, health-focused water purifier, leveraging Aquaporin's existing user-friendly design and brand reputation. Begin with a limited launch in a specific segment (e.g., health-conscious households) to test demand before broader rollout.
final.target_customer: Health-conscious consumers who prioritize higher purity and better taste in drinking water and are willing to pay a premium for a premium positioning.
final.value_proposition: A premium-priced water purifier that emphasizes superior taste, purity, and ease of use, offering a differentiated experience compared to standard models.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Premium vs. Sustainability Messaging Test (300 participants, 6 weeks, €15,000) to validate purchase intent and willingness-to-pay differences between premium health and sustainability messaging.
final.uncertainty: The evidence base is limited to company claims and a single simulated test; no independent consumer survey data exists. The financial and market constraints of Aquaporin are also unknown from public sources.
would_change_if: If the test shows the sustainability messaging version achieving at least 15% higher purchase intent and 10% higher average WTP than the premium health messaging version, we would shift focus to a sustainability proposition.
If the premium health messaging version fails to meet the threshold, we would reconsider the premium positioning and explore alternative value propositions.

result.title: Simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

Each participant views a product description of a differentiated Aquaporin water purifier (same specs, price, and brand positioning). Participants are then asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 300 participants (150 per condition) from a panel of health‑conscious and environmentally conscious consumers in Denmark and Germany.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price willingness to pay for the differentiated purifier.

In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 60 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 120 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient public evidence to justify Aquaporin A/S investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current water-membrane offering.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or a viable route to market for a differentiated consumer proposition.
Any recommendation must be based on observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., home water purifier for a niche segment).

T1.who_benefits: Health‑conscious consumers seeking higher purity and better taste in drinking water.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If consumers shift from viewing water purifiers as a necessity to a lifestyle or health product, they will be willing to purchase a premium‑priced purifier that justifies the cost.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Aquaporin can capture value by pricing the differentiated product at a premium, selling through direct‑to‑consumer channels or premium retailers, and leveraging brand positioning as a premium water‑purification solution.
assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay more for perceived health and taste benefits.
The premium positioning can be effectively communicated to the target segment.
Distribution channels can reach the premium segment without significant cost.
predictions: In a test offering a premium‑priced differentiated purifier, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a standard‑priced model.
Surveyed consumers will rank taste and purity as top reasons for purchasing the premium product.

tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 120 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 60 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

X1.name: Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants view one of two product descriptions of a differentiated home water purifier (premium taste/purity vs sustainability/eco-friendly). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 500 adult consumers in Denmark and Turkey, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to see either the premium messaging or the sustainability messaging.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for the premium messaging version.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for the sustainability messaging version.

X1.decision_rule: If the premium messaging version achieves a purchase intent score at least 5 points higher than the sustainability messaging version AND the difference in maximum price willingness to pay is at least €20, proceed to develop the premium positioning. If the sustainability messaging version achieves the same or higher score, proceed to develop the sustainability positioning. If neither condition is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

revisions.reason: The simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test (SYN-AQP-UPDATE) does not address consumer motivations for a differentiated home water purifier. It tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under a conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, taste, purity, or sustainability. Therefore it does not affect T1.

Begin with a limited pilot in Denmark and Turkey to test purchase intent and price sensitivity before scaling.

final.value_proposition: A premium, easy‑to‑use home water purifier that delivers superior taste and purity, with minimal maintenance and a user‑friendly design, justified by a premium price point.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test (500 participants, 8 weeks, €15,000) to compare purchase intent and price willingness under premium and sustainability messaging.

arguments.name: Premium vs Sustainability Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants view one of two product descriptions of a differentiated home water purifier (premium taste/purity vs sustainability/eco-friendly). They are then asked to indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and maximum price they would pay.
arguments.sample: 500 adult consumers in Denmark and Turkey, recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income. Randomly assigned to see either the premium messaging or the sustainability messaging.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and maximum price willingness to pay.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for the premium messaging version.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and higher maximum price for the sustainability messaging version.

arguments.decision_rule: If the premium messaging version achieves a purchase intent score at least 5 points higher than the sustainability messaging version AND the difference in maximum price willingness to pay is at least €20, proceed to develop the premium positioning. If the sustainability messaging version achieves the same or higher score, proceed to develop the sustainability positioning. If neither condition is met, do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.
