result.title: Simulated maintenance-convenience proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 120 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 60 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. An unchanged business recommendation can be justified by those other constraints.

In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 households already using a compatible drinking-water purifier received the same membrane specifications, water-quality information, brand, warranty and total annual price. Half were offered a prepaid plan with scheduled cartridge delivery and replacement reminders; half were offered a prepaid self-service cartridge plan without that delivery schedule or reminders. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid plan enrollment remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned households per arm. This what-if assumes an authorised operator can legally supply and service the offer; it does not change the dossier evidence about Aquaporin's insolvency or financing. There were 120 plan enrollments in the scheduled-delivery-and-reminder plan arm and 60 in the self-service cartridge plan arm. This tests willingness to enroll in a maintenance offer under that conditional supply assumption, not membrane efficacy, correct long-term filter use, market size, company solvency or Aquaporin's ability to fund an offer. T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers currently obtain espresso at home through pre-portioned pods or instant coffee. A differentiated proposition that allows precise control and authentic brewing would shift their preference from convenience to quality and sociality.

arguments.who_benefits: Home baristas seeking a professional-level experience and the broader community of coffee enthusiasts.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers currently obtain espresso at home through pre-portioned pods or instant coffee. A differentiated proposition that allows precise control and authentic brewing would shift their preference from convenience to quality and sociality.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Simonelli can charge a premium price for a differentiated machine and accessories, and potentially license its brand for community-focused content or services.
assumptions: Consumers value the ritual and skill of espresso making over convenience.
There is a large, underserved segment of home baristas willing to invest in premium equipment.
Simonelli can produce a differentiated product within budget and time constraints.
predictions: A test offering a differentiated home machine will generate higher purchase intent among self-identified home baristas compared to a standard compact machine.
Surveyed consumers will rank the ability to make authentic espresso as their top purchase criterion for a home machine.

arguments.claim: Home barista demand is driven by the need for convenience and time savings, particularly among busy professionals and small offices. If Simonelli Group creates a consumer proposition that emphasizes quick, easy espresso preparation, consumers will adopt it as a time-saving solution.
arguments.who_benefits: Busy professionals and small office environments seeking efficient coffee solutions.
arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers currently spend time measuring water, grinding beans, and waiting for espresso. A differentiated proposition that automates or simplifies the brewing process would shift their preference from ritual to convenience.
arguments.how_value_is_captured: Simonelli can capture value through higher volume sales of compact, automated machines and accessories, and potentially through subscription services for maintenance or coffee pods.
assumptions: Time is a primary constraint for home coffee preparation.
Consumers are willing to trade some ritual for convenience.
Simonelli can develop a compact, automated product within budget and time constraints.
predictions: A test offering a compact, automated home machine will show higher purchase intent among busy professionals compared to a standard compact machine.
Surveyed consumers will rank time savings as their top purchase criterion for a home machine.

frame.objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.
Alternatives include expanding the existing professional line, creating a new consumer product, targeting a different customer segment, or maintaining the current portfolio.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home barista, travel, or small office) with a new product or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing professional line with consumer‑focused features (e.g., simplified controls, compact design) without creating a new product.
3) Target a different customer segment (e.g., coffee shops, hotels, or retail consumers) with a differentiated offering, leveraging existing or new distribution channels.
4) Maintain the current portfolio and not pursue expansion, focusing resources on existing professional and commercial segments.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers substitute the café for home use because the café offers a third place for social interaction, which they cannot replicate at home. This shifts purchase motivation from pure coffee quality to the social experience.

Consumers are willing to pay more for machines that signal social status and a curated coffee experience.
Simonelli can effectively communicate the social aspect of its machines to consumers.
predictions: In a test offering a premium-priced home barista machine with social branding, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard professional machine.
Surveyed home baristas will rank social experience as a top factor in purchase decisions.
Willingness to pay for the social aspect will exceed willingness to pay for functional improvements alone.

frame.objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.
Alternatives include expanding the existing professional line, creating a new consumer product, targeting a different customer segment, or maintaining the current portfolio.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home barista, travel, or small office) with a new product or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing professional line with consumer‑focused features (e.g., simplified controls, compact design) without creating a new product.
3) Target a different customer segment (e.g., coffee shops, hotels, or retail consumers) with a differentiated offering, leveraging existing or new distribution channels.
4) Maintain the current portfolio and not pursue expansion, focusing resources on existing professional and commercial segments.

T1.claim: Home barista consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they view coffee as a lifestyle experience and are willing to pay a premium for quality and convenience.
T1.who_benefits: Home barista consumers seeking a premium coffee experience.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They shift from generic coffee to a specialized machine that offers consistent quality, ease of use, and design, making coffee preparation a enjoyable activity rather than a chore.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Simonelli can capture value through premium pricing, brand positioning as a lifestyle product, and potential cross-selling of accessories or subscription services.
assumptions: Home barista market is growing despite economic uncertainty.
Consumers are willing to invest in high-quality coffee equipment.
Simonelli can effectively communicate the lifestyle value of its products.
predictions: Surveyed home barista consumers will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% more for a differentiated machine compared to standard models.
Sales of a differentiated consumer line will exceed a baseline of 500 units within the first year in a target market.
T1.first_claim: Home barista consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition because they view coffee as a lifestyle experience and are willing to pay a premium for quality and convenience.

T2.claim: Simonelli Group will not develop a differentiated consumer proposition because the home barista market is small and unprofitable, and the company prioritizes its professional and commercial segments.
T2.who_benefits: Simonelli Group's existing professional and commercial customers who already purchase its machines.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: The company lacks the market size and margin to justify investment in a new consumer product, and its resources are better allocated to higher-margin professional segments.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Simonelli can capture value by maintaining its current revenue streams and avoiding capital expenditure on a consumer line that may not generate sufficient returns.
assumptions: The home barista market is not large enough to support a profitable consumer line.
Simonelli's current professional and commercial segments generate higher margins than consumer products.
The company has limited capacity to develop and market a new consumer product.
predictions: Simonelli's revenue from professional and commercial segments will continue to grow at a rate higher than consumer sales.
A proposed consumer line will not achieve a break-even point within the 12-week test period.
Simonelli will not allocate additional resources to develop a consumer product.

frame.objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.
Alternatives include expanding the existing professional line, creating a new consumer product, targeting a different customer segment, or maintaining the current portfolio.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home barista, travel, or small office) with a new product or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing professional line with consumer‑focused features (e.g., simplified controls, compact design) without creating a new product.
3) Target a different customer segment (e.g., coffee shops, hotels, or retail consumers) with a differentiated offering, leveraging existing or new distribution channels.
4) Maintain the current portfolio and not pursue expansion, focusing resources on existing professional and commercial segments.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers shift from professional equipment to home use when they view the product as convenient and stylish, reducing perceived complexity and increasing leisure value.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Simonelli can command premium pricing for design, materials, and brand positioning, and potentially cross-sell accessories or subscription services.

X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants view a product description of a compact, entry-level home barista machine (Simonelli) and are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2‑ very unlikely to 7‑2‑ very likely). They are also asked about maximum willingness to pay and a brief qualitative reason.
X1.sample: 300 adult respondents recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and age to reflect home barista demographics. Recruitment target: self-identified home baristas or coffee enthusiasts aged 25–45.
X1.measure: 1) Average purchase intent score (mean of 7-point scale). 2) Maximum willingness to pay (highest stated price). 3) Qualitative reason for purchase intent (open-ended).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Average purchase intent ≥ 5.5 and willingness to pay ≥ €1,200, with ease of use and design cited as primary drivers.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Average purchase intent ≤ 4.5 and willingness to pay ≤ €1,000, with respondents citing market decline or lack of perceived need as reasons.

X1.decision_rule: If average purchase intent ≥ 5.5 and willingness to pay ≥ €1,200, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If average purchase intent ≤ 4.5 and willingness to pay ≤ €1,000, do not invest in a consumer expansion. If intent is between 4.5 and 5.5 and willingness to pay is between €1,000 and €1,200, conduct a smaller test of willingness to pay and design.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

T1.claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if they perceive it as a premium, professional-grade cooking tool that saves time and delivers consistent results, because they value convenience and quality in their kitchen.
T1.who_benefits: Home cooks who cook frequently and want efficient, high-quality cooking solutions.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They shift from traditional cooking methods to a single appliance that combines steaming, boiling, and other functions, reducing the need for multiple devices and simplifying meal preparation.
T1.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL can charge a premium price for a differentiated product, sell through specialty retailers or online channels, and capture recurring revenue through accessories or subscription services.
assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay a premium for a professional-grade cooking system.
The combi-steamer's features (e.g., steam control, temperature precision) are perceived as superior to traditional methods.
Marketing can effectively communicate the professional-grade benefits to home cooks.
predictions: In a test offering a differentiated combi-steamer at a premium price, purchase intent among home cooks will be higher than for a standard model.
Surveyed home cooks will rank the product higher for convenience and quality compared to a comparable entry-level model.
T1.first_claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if they perceive it as a premium, professional-grade cooking tool that saves time and delivers consistent results, because they value convenience and quality in their kitchen.

T2.claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is marketed as a subscription-based service that delivers recipes, meal prep guidance, and maintenance, because they seek convenience and personalized cooking support.
T2.who_benefits: Home cooks who prefer hands‑off cooking solutions and value ongoing guidance.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: They shift from traditional cooking methods to a service that automates meal planning, preparation, and maintenance, reducing the time and effort required to cook.
T2.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL can monetize through recurring subscription fees, sell premium accessories, and capture data for personalized recommendations, creating a recurring revenue stream.
assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay a monthly subscription for cooking support.
The service's content (recipes, guidance) is perceived as valuable and engaging.
The subscription model can be scaled without compromising product quality.
predictions: In a test offering a subscription‑based combi-steamer, monthly active users will increase over time compared to a product‑only offering.
Surveyed home cooks will indicate higher satisfaction with the service's convenience and personalization than with a standard product.

position.recommendation: Develop a differentiated home proposition for time‑constrained home cooks, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing combi‑steamer technology. The evidence shows RATIONAL already serves commercial kitchens and has a large market potential, but no source directly addresses home cook motivations. The proposed test (X1) would clarify whether convenience drives demand, which would justify the investment.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

T1.claim: Home cooks buy combi-steamers primarily for convenience and time savings, not as a status or fashion item. If RATIONAL introduces a differentiated home proposition, they will adopt it because it reduces cooking time and simplifies meal preparation, but the demand will be limited to users who already cook frequently and value efficiency.
T1.who_benefits: Time‑constrained home cooks who cook multiple meals daily and prefer quick, hands‑off cooking.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They switch from traditional cooking methods (e.g., pots, ovens) to a single device that steams and cooks simultaneously, eliminating multiple appliances and reducing prep time.
T1.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL can charge a premium for a compact, smart, or subscription‑based home unit, leveraging its existing commercial brand and distribution to reach residential buyers.
assumptions: Home cooks currently own multiple cooking appliances and are willing to replace them with a single, high‑performance device.
The target market is large enough to justify production and marketing investment.
Consumers perceive the time‑saving benefit as a primary purchase driver.
predictions: In a test offering a compact, smart combi‑steamer to a sample of home cooks, purchase intent will be higher than for a standard commercial unit.
Willingness to pay will be above the cost of a comparable commercial unit, indicating a price premium for convenience.
Adoption will be concentrated among users who cook multiple meals daily and have limited kitchen space.

X1.sample: 500 home cooks recruited via an online panel, balanced across the three groups (166 per group).

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: The simulated result (SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE) tests whether installation coordination changes choice among home cooks. It does not address home cook motivations (convenience vs. health), so it neither supports nor contradicts T1. The theory remains unchanged.
arguments.new_claim: Home cooks buy combi-steamers primarily for convenience and time savings, not as a status or fashion item. If RATIONAL introduces a differentiated home proposition, they will adopt it because it reduces cooking time and simplifies meal preparation, but the demand will be limited to users who already cook frequently and value efficiency.

arguments.recommendation: Develop a differentiated home proposition for time‑constrained home cooks, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing combi‑steamer technology. The proposed test (X1) would clarify whether convenience drives demand, which would justify the investment.
arguments.target_customer: Time‑constrained home cooks who cook multiple meals daily and value efficiency.
arguments.value_proposition: A compact, smart combi‑steamer that reduces cooking time and simplifies meal preparation, positioned as a single, high‑performance device replacing multiple appliances.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed 8‑week, €18,000 messaging test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for convenience‑focused messaging.
arguments.uncertainty: The source does not address home cook motivations, so the demand for a differentiated home proposition remains uncertain. The test will resolve this uncertainty.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent below 7.5 or willingness to pay below the standard commercial unit price by ≥ 15%, the recommendation would shift to stay focused on professional kitchens.
If additional evidence shows strong health or nutrition motivations among home cooks, the recommendation would shift toward a health‑focused proposition.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

T1.claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is marketed as a smart, subscription-based device that automates cooking and delivers recipes, because they value convenience and recurring revenue.
T1.who_benefits: Home cooks gain time and reduced effort; RATIONAL benefits from recurring subscription revenue and premium pricing.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Smart home integration and subscription model reduce upfront cost and provide ongoing value, making the appliance attractive to tech-savvy consumers.
T1.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL captures value through subscription fees and premium pricing for smart features, while also leveraging its existing B2B reputation to build trust.
assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay a subscription fee for convenience.
Smart home integration is accessible and affordable to residential users.
RATIONAL can adapt its commercial technology to a residential subscription model without significant redesign.
predictions: A test offering a subscription-based smart combi-steamer will generate at least 10% monthly recurring revenue from a sample of 500 home cooks within 12 weeks.
Surveyed participants will rate the device 7/10 or higher on convenience and willingness to pay a monthly fee.
T1.first_claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is marketed as a smart, subscription-based device that automates cooking and delivers recipes, because they value convenience and recurring revenue.

T2.claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is positioned as a premium, high-performance appliance that emphasizes professional-grade cooking performance, because they seek superior results and are willing to pay for it.
T2.who_benefits: Home cooks gain professional-quality cooking results; RATIONAL benefits from premium pricing and brand prestige.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers with professional cooking aspirations view the appliance as a status symbol and a tool for achieving restaurant-quality results, leading them to choose it over generic devices.
T2.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL captures value through premium pricing, limited-edition designs, and brand positioning as a professional-grade brand, while also leveraging its existing B2B reputation.
assumptions: Home cooks have professional cooking aspirations and are willing to pay a premium for performance.
Professional-grade positioning can be effectively communicated to residential consumers without diluting the brand.
RATIONAL can maintain its professional kitchen reputation while creating a differentiated residential offering.
predictions: A test offering a premium, high-performance combi-steamer will achieve at least 15% higher purchase intent among home cooks compared to a standard model, measured through a survey of 500 home cooks within 12 weeks.
Participants will rank the premium model 8/10 or higher on performance and be willing to pay at least 20% more than the standard model.

constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

X1.name: Smart vs Premium Combi-Steamer Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from a panel of home cooks (n=300). They are shown two identical product descriptions of a RATIONAL combi-steamer, differing only in messaging: one emphasizes smart home integration and subscription convenience (T1), the other emphasizes professional-grade precision and premium design (T2). Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and whether they would pay a subscription fee (if T1).
X1.sample: 300 adult home cooks recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and region.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and willingness to pay a subscription fee (binary: ≥ €10/month).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and subscription willingness among participants shown the smart positioning message.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and subscription willingness among participants shown the premium positioning message.

X1.decision_rule: If the mean purchase intent for the smart positioning group is at least 1.5 points higher than the mean for the premium positioning group, and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), proceed with a smart‑focused differentiated proposition. If the premium positioning group’s mean is at least 1.5 points higher, and the difference is statistically significant, proceed with a premium‑focused proposition. If neither difference meets the threshold, do not expand into either segment.

arguments.name: Smart vs Premium Combi-Steamer Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging. Participants are recruited from a panel of home cooks (n=300). They are shown two identical product descriptions of a RATIONAL combi-steamer, differing only in messaging: one emphasizes smart home integration and subscription convenience (T1), the other emphasizes professional-grade precision and premium design (T2). Participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and whether they would pay a subscription fee (if T1).
arguments.sample: 300 adult home cooks recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and region.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and willingness to pay a subscription fee (binary: ≥ €10/month).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and subscription willingness among participants shown the smart positioning message.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and subscription willingness among participants shown the premium positioning message.

arguments.decision_rule: If the mean purchase intent for the smart positioning group is at least 1.5 points higher than the mean for the premium positioning group, and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), proceed with a smart‑focused differentiated proposition. If the premium positioning group’s mean is at least 1.5 points higher, and the difference is statistically significant, proceed with a premium‑focused proposition. If neither difference meets the threshold, do not expand into either segment.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

T1.claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is marketed as a smart, subscription-based device that automates cooking and delivers recipes, because they value convenience and recurring revenue.
T1.who_benefits: Home cooks seeking time-saving, automated cooking solutions.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: They would switch from traditional ovens or stovetops to a device that learns their preferences and sends recipe suggestions, reducing manual effort and decision fatigue.
T1.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL can charge a monthly subscription for recipe access, software updates, and premium features, generating recurring revenue while leveraging its existing combi-steamer technology.
assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay a recurring fee for smart cooking assistance.
The subscription model is feasible without disrupting the core combi-steamer functionality.
Marketing can effectively communicate the convenience and automation benefits to residential users.
predictions: A survey of home cooks would show at least 30% indicating intent to subscribe to a smart combi-steamer at a price point of $150-$200 per month.
Pilot adoption would increase in households with children or busy lifestyles compared to non-pilot households.
T1.first_claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is marketed as a smart, subscription-based device that automates cooking and delivers recipes, because they value convenience and recurring revenue.

T2.claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is positioned as a premium, high-performance appliance that offers superior cooking performance and durability, because they value professional-quality results and are willing to pay a premium for it.
T2.who_benefits: Home cooks who prioritize professional cooking outcomes and are willing to invest in high-end appliances.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: They would switch from entry-level or traditional appliances to a device that delivers consistent, high-quality results, reducing the need for multiple cookware items and time spent troubleshooting.
T2.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL can charge a premium price for advanced features, durability, and brand prestige, while also offering warranty and service that differentiates it from budget alternatives.
assumptions: Home cooks have a willingness to pay a premium for professional-grade performance.
The premium positioning can be effectively communicated through marketing and brand storytelling.
Durability and reliability are key purchase drivers for this segment.
predictions: A survey of home cooks would show at least 25% indicating intent to purchase a premium combi-steamer at a price of $800-$1,200, compared to 15% for a standard model.
Pilot adoption would be higher among households with a higher disposable income and a history of purchasing premium kitchen appliances.

X1.name: Home Cook Preference Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized product exposure and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
X1.sample: 500 home cooks recruited via a panel, balanced for age, gender, and cooking frequency.
X1.measure: 1) Purchase intent: "Would you buy this differentiated combi-steamer at a premium price?" (binary: Yes/No). 2) WTP premium: "How much more would you pay for this compared to a standard model?" (EUR). 3) Subscription preference: "Would you subscribe to a monthly recipe/service for this combi-steamer?" (binary: Yes/No).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher WTP premium for the differentiated premium model than for a standard model.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher subscription preference and higher WTP for the subscription-based model than for the product-only model.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent for the differentiated premium model exceeds 40% and its WTP premium exceeds 20% of the standard model's price, proceed with a differentiated premium home-cook proposition. If subscription preference exceeds 40% and WTP for the subscription model exceeds 20% of the premium model's price, pursue a subscription model. If neither condition is met, stay with professional kitchens.

revisions.reason: The simulated installation-coordination offer test (SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE) does not address home cook preferences, premium pricing, or subscription models. It tests a narrow coordination mechanism (installation friction) and does not establish market size, hardware need, or value capture for a differentiated combi-steamer. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Develop a differentiated premium home-cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription-based combi-steamer) targeting frequent home cooks who value professional-grade convenience and quality.
final.target_customer: Home cooks who cook frequently and want efficient, high-quality cooking solutions, particularly those who currently use multiple cooking devices.
final.value_proposition: A premium, professional-grade combi-steamer that combines steaming, boiling, and other functions in a single appliance, offering convenience, consistent results, and potential for recurring revenue through accessories or subscription.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Home Cook Preference Test (500 respondents, 8 weeks, €18,000) to validate purchase intent and willingness-to-pay for a differentiated premium model versus a standard model.
final.uncertainty: The size of the home-cook market, willingness to pay a premium, and the effectiveness of a subscription model remain uncertain. The test will clarify these points before committing resources.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent below 40% or WTP premium below 20% of the standard model's price, we would abandon the premium home-cook proposition and stay focused on professional kitchens.
If the test demonstrates strong subscription preference and WTP for a subscription model, we would pursue a subscription-based model.
If new evidence shows home cooks prefer entry-level appliances over premium professional-grade devices, we would reconsider the premium positioning.

arguments.name: Home Cook Preference Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized product exposure and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.
arguments.sample: 500 home cooks recruited via a panel, balanced for age, gender, and cooking frequency.
arguments.measure: 1) Purchase intent: "Would you buy this differentiated combi-steamer at a premium price?" (binary: Yes/No). 2) WTP premium: "How much more would you pay for this compared to a standard model?" (EUR). 3) Subscription preference: "Would you subscribe to a monthly recipe/service for this combi-steamer?" (binary: Yes/No).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and higher WTP premium for the differentiated premium model than for a standard model.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher subscription preference and higher WTP for the subscription-based model than for the product-only model.

arguments.decision_rule: If purchase intent for the differentiated premium model exceeds 40% and its WTP premium exceeds 20% of the standard model's price, proceed with a differentiated premium home-cook proposition. If subscription preference exceeds 40% and WTP for the subscription model exceeds 20% of the premium model's price, pursue a subscription model. If neither condition is met, stay with professional kitchens.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Develop a differentiated premium home-cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription-based combi-steamer) targeting frequent home cooks who value professional-grade convenience and quality.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: The simulated installation-coordination offer test (SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE) does not address home cook preferences, premium pricing, or subscription models. It tests a narrow coordination mechanism (installation friction) and does not establish market size, hardware need, or value capture for a differentiated combi-steamer. Therefore it does not affect T1.

arguments.recommendation: Develop a differentiated premium home-cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription-based combi-steamer) targeting frequent home cooks who value professional-grade convenience and quality.
arguments.target_customer: Home cooks who cook frequently and want efficient, high-quality cooking solutions, particularly those who currently use multiple cooking devices.
arguments.value_proposition: A premium, professional-grade combi-steamer that combines steaming, boiling, and other functions in a single appliance, offering convenience, consistent results, and potential for recurring revenue through accessories or subscription.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Home Cook Preference Test (500 respondents, 8 weeks, €18,000) to validate purchase intent and willingness-to-pay for a differentiated premium model versus a standard model.
arguments.uncertainty: The size of the home-cook market, willingness to pay a premium, and the effectiveness of a subscription model remain uncertain. The test will clarify these points before committing resources.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent below 40% or WTP premium below 20% of the standard model's price, we would abandon the premium home-cook proposition and stay focused on professional kitchens.
If the test demonstrates strong subscription preference and WTP for a subscription model, we would pursue a subscription-based model.
If new evidence shows home cooks prefer entry-level appliances over premium professional-grade devices, we would reconsider the premium positioning.
